2. Short relevant facts leading to the filing of this revisional application is that, the opposite party No. 1, as sole plaintiff, filed Title Suit No. 29 of 1971, in the 1 st Court of Subordinate Judge, against the petitioner and others for a declaration of his Junglebari Abadkari right on reclamation and confirmation of possession therein and also for permanent injunction. The said suit on transfer was renumbered as Title Suit No. 3 of 1976. During the pendency of the said title suit plaintiff-opposite party Nos. 2-9 filed a petition under Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure to be impleaded as plaintiffs in the said suit. The prayer was allowed. The plaintiffs assert that the land in question originally belonged to Baraura Tea Company Ltd. within Rashidpur Tea Estate. The plaintiff No. 1 took lease for the year 1360 BS on annual rental thereof. Plaintiffs assert that after taking Amaldari from the Manager of the said Tea Company and clearing the jungles, plaintiff No. 1 was possessing the same without any interruption or obstruction. That defendant No. 1, Government of Bangladesh, served a notice of eviction under Act 10 of 1953 and being threatened he filed TS 218 of 1968. The said suit was dismissed on contest. Thereafter, the said plaintiff No. 1 preferred an appeal which subsequently was withdrawn with the leave of the Court to file a suit afresh. 

 3. The case of the petitioner Government is that the land originally belonged to Rashidpur Tea Estate Co. and the said Tea Estate Company surrendered the excess of khas land including the land in the suit and the Government took over the same. Compensation of the surrendered land including the suit land was also assessed. That the plaintiff is in unauthorised possession of the suit land. So notice was issued for his eviction and that the land having been vested in Govt. in pursuance of wholesale acquisition of tenancy, vested in the Government and the Government acquired the same free from all encumbrances. 

 5. Mr. Syed JR Modassir Hossain, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the petitioner, submits that the Court of appeal below committed an error of law in not adverting to the findings of the learned trial Court with proper and sound reasonings. Mr. Hossain argues that the learned Court of Appeal below has committed serious error of law in not considering the basic documents filed by the defendant Government such as Exhibits 'A', 'B', 'H' and 'K' which would positively indicate that the land in question and all the land surrendered to the Government by that Tea Estate as excess of khas lands had vested in the Government. Mr. Modassir Hossain also argues that there are errors of law on the face of record and as such the impugned judgment and decree must be set aside. 

 14. In the plaint, the plaintiff No.1 Md. Aslam as the sole plaintiff averred that he is the 16 annas owner of the suit land and had acquired the same from the Rashidpur Tea Estate on receipt of rent-receipts for clearing jungle and bushes and had been exercising "Abadkari Amaldari right". That on the expiry of the said Amaldari right on 29.9.1955, the plaintiff wrote to the Manager for renewal of the settlement and the Manager granted Amaldari letter dated 15.10.55 and thereafter by Amaldari letter dated 1.10.1957 renewed the term. He asserted that he himself acquired such right and settlement was taken in his name and he paid the rents by himself. That subsequently he filed Title Suit No. 218 of 1966 and ultimately withdrew the suit and appeal at the appellate stage with permission of the appellate Court to file a suit afresh. And he filed the present suit for a declaration of his Junglebari Abadkari right by reclamation as well as right by adverse possession and that the defendant had no right in the suit land and confirmation of possession. He also made a prayer for permanent injunction against the Government. It may be noted that the Rashidpur Tea Estate or for that matter the Baraura Tea Company Limited is not made a party in this suit. 

 17. PW 1 Abdul Latif in his deposition stated that the lands in the suit in question were acquired by way of settlement by all the nine plaintiffs, rents were paid by them and they jointly possessed the lands. He further filed a registered partition deed dated 5.4.72 showing the suit lands were divided amongst all the nine plaintiffs on different shares mentioned in the said deed. The partition deed is made Ext.7. 

 19. The plaintiff must not make any departure from the earlier pleadings made in the plaint so as to bring into existence any new claim or raise any new ground or plea which are quite inconsistent, incongruous or a departure from the earlier stand or pleas. The Court will not allow either party from making any departure from the earlier pleadings set forth in the plaint or written statement. Plaint and written statement are the foundation of the claim of the plaintiff and the defendant; any deviation from the earlier stand would surely land the other side into serious dislocation and by Order 6 rule 7 of the Civil Procedure Code the same has been made prohibited. 

 Ext. 1 (a) another rent receipt in an ordinary typed paper dated 15.10.1955 signed by Manager, Reshidpur Tea Estate for the year 1361 BS. 

 26. The plaintiff has filed the suit with the assertion that the plots in dispute were settled with him on the basis of the rent receipts granted by the Baraura Tea Company who was a rent receiver. It is found by the learned Judge, and also contended by the learned Advocate for the plaintiff opposite parties that the said rent receipts were acted upon and the plaintiff held over the possession by acquiring Abadkari Amaldari right. It is to be noted that this Abadkari Amaldari right is unknown or unrecognised by the State Acquisition &Tenancy Act. Section 2 of the Act defines various types of right or tenancy recognised by the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. By the word 'Amaldari' it is meant a writ authorising the grantee to take possession and there by Amaldari at best one can gain a possessory interest without any semblance to title. 

 27. Section 101 of the Evidence Act, requires that the plaintiff who wants the Court to believe that the alleged receipts have created any right or title in his favour or any legal right or liability has been created by virtue of such settlement by way of those rent-receipts, it is the plaintiff who has to prove the same in a legal manner as provided under the Act. Whether these rent receipts were genuine or represented true and correct state of things, the burden of proving such things heavily lies on the plaintiff. It is to be noted that no witness has been examined to prove the rent receipts, the alleged signature of the Manager of the Tea Company Limited or the contents of such rent-receipts. Without such proof the rent-receipts Ext. 1, 1(a), 1(b) and Ext. 2 cannot be accepted as legally proved or exhibited. The learned Judge thus has committed a serious error of law in taking into consideration and based his decision on the rent-receipts in matter of title which 'affected the merit of the casco Mere filing a rent receipt or a private document without formal proof thereof and without proving the contents of such documents cannot fulfill the requirements of section 101 and section 103 of the Evidence Act. Therefore, in my view, by Ext. 1, 1(a), 1(b) and Ext. 2, the plaintiff has acquired no title. 

 "In this case the plaintiffs have come to the Court with the assertion that the disputed land was settled with them by the owners of the land on the basis of the Kabuliyat Ext. 3(a) and produced the Dakhilas Ext. 4 series in proof of the fact that the Kabuliyat was acted upon on subsequent payment of rent in pursuance of the said settlement. According to section 101 of the Act, as referred to above, it is for the plaintiffs to prove that as a matter of fact, settlement was granted by the owners of the land and the rent receipts Ext. 4 series were really genuine and represented the correct state of things, as the plaintiffs desire the Court to believe on the said assertion. The burden of proof as to the genuineness of the dakhila Ext. 4 series is undoubtedly upon them in the absence of any legislative provision to the contrary. There having been no legislative enactment requiring the dakhilas, Ext. 4 series, which had been formally proved at the trial of the suit, to be accepted as genuine documents, merely on proof thereof there is no question of shifting the onus upon the defendants. The learned Judges of the High Court appears to have been under a misapprehension as to the real effect of formal proof of a document in a Court of law. A private document cannot be taken notice of and marked as an exhibit without any formal proof, unless the requirement of such proof is waived by the opposing party. The marking of the said document as an exhibit may, however, give rise to a belief that it bears the writing or signature of a person as has been deposed to by the witness who proves the said document. The question as to whether the document is a genuine one or it represents the true state of affairs is a question of fact which is to be decided by the Court concerned in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case. There is no legal presumption which the Court is bound to make in respect of such a document. There may be cases where the law requires that the contents of a particular document shall be presumed to be correct unless they are rebutted by adducing evidence by a party who disputes their correctness, as has been provided in section I03B of the Bengal Tenancy Act and section 144A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950. There is no such law as requires a Court to presume that a rent receipt purported to be granted by a landlord in favour of a certain person is genuine and what has been written in such a rent receipt are true. The learned Judges of the High Court have apparently made a mistake in taking the view that as soon as the rent receipts have been proved the primary onus of the plaintiffs has been discharged and the defendants having failed to produce any rebutting evidence the said rent receipts should have been accepted as genuine and relied upon. The onus of the plaintiffs cannot be discharged until the Court is persuaded to accept the position that there had been payment of rent by the tenant and acceptance thereof by the landlord, as a matter of fact on the basis of the disputed rent receipts. In this case both of the Courts of fact have decided the question of genuineness of the disputed rent receipts in the light of the facts and circumstances of the case and have also examined their various features with reference to the surrounding facts and came to the definite finding as to their spurious character. Such a finding is binding upon the High Court in a Second Appeal unless it could be shown the said finding had been vitiated by an error of law or of procedure which had affected the merits of the case."

Ext. 2, the alleged basic lease letter granted by the Rashidpur Tea Estate dated 15.9.1955 leasing out the suit property for a period of two years is hit by section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act as not being registered. Unregistered lease deed of immovable property from year to year is inadmissible in evidence for lack of registration. 

 32. Mr. JR Modassir Hossain, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the petitioner, submits that Court of appeal' below committed an error of law in not taking into consideration the material documents filed by the Government in support of their claim. He submits that Exhibit 'A', statement of excess lands of the Tea Estate surrendered under section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act to the Government under Memo No. 989/SA dated 29.8.74; 

 Exhibit 'B' the certificate in Misc. Case No, 9 of 1972 under sub-section 4(a) of section 20 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 by ADC (Rev.) Sylhet; 

 33. State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into force by publication of notification No. 4829 LR dated 2nd April, 1956, published in the Dhaka Gazelle Extraordinary dated 2nd April, 1956. The Government have acquired by notification in the official gazette all the interests of land of rent receivers as specified in the notification in the respective Taluks, Tenures, holding or tenancy and all interest in any estate, Taluk or holdings in the khas possession of the tenure holders. UR4er sub-section 

 (1) of section 3 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, Government acquires interest of the proprietors, tenure holders and rent receivers including khas lands (beyond the retainable limit) by publication of notification from the date mentioned therein and these interests vest in the Government absolutely free from all encumbrances. By Exhibit 'R' Baraura Tea Estate through their Manager surrendered the excess khas land to the Government. The learned trial Court found that the excess land so surrendered by Baraura Tea Co. Ltd. in favour of the Government was duly accepted by the Government and compensation assessment' roll was also published. Rent-receivers having khas lands in the capacity of a rent receiver are stripped of their excess khas lands on the very moment of the publication of notification under sub-section 1 of section 3, and the same vests in the Government absolutely free from all encumbrances. It may be noted that the lands in schedule of the plaint falls within surrendered excess khas land. It may also be noted that the records of right and the compensation roll were prepared in the name of the Baraura Tea Company and not in the name of the plaintiff. Had the plaintiff occupied the lands in question as a rayati or under rayati, record of right or the compensation roll would also have been prepared in his name and the Baraura Tea Company would definitely have excluded the plots in question from the lands surrendered as in the statement Ext. 'H'. 

 34. The scheme of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, would reveal that special provision has been made in Chapter II of Part-II of the Act in regard to acquisition of rent-receiving interests and special provision for acquisition of the interests of certain rent-receivers. According to this provision, rent-receiving interest can be acquired by notification under section 3 of the Act even before the general provisions of the aforesaid Act have been given effect to. Before acquisition of the interests of the rent-receivers and tenure holders or Taluks or rayati or the khas lands of the tenure holders or rent-receivers, preparation of the record of rights is necessary. Thereafter, the compensation assessment roll is prepared and published in order to give effect to such provision of law. Sub-section 2(a) in section 3 of the Act was introduced by amendment empowering the Government to publish notification in respect of rent-receiver by name with reference to areas where such interests exist in the manner the Government might determine and notifications were issued District-wise but the rent-receiving interests and vesting of khas lands in the Government shall vest in the Government with effect from 14.4.1956 in terms of those notification issued. 

 36. As to adverse possession claimed by the plaintiffs in matter of acquisition of title, it is to be borne in mind that in order to acquire title by exercise of adverse possession, the same must be open, hostile and within the knowledge of the real owner for over statutory period of limitation. The learned appellate Judge declared title in favour of the plaintiff by adverse possession against the Tea Company who is not even a party in the suit and the Tea Company long before has been divested of its right, title and possession by surrendering the excess khas land in favour of the Government and thereby extinguished all its right and title. But as against the Government the learned appellate Judge did not utter a word, although Government is the defendant No.1 and the real contestant over the suit lands. As against Government the limitation for acquisition of tide by adverse possession is 60 years which is a far cry for the plaintiff to establish. The finding of the learned Judge is palpably wrong.
